Dado que son un solo Dios, podemos entender aquí una referencia al Padre; La acción de Dios es la acción de cada una de las tres personas. Dios sostiene todas las cosas por su Palabra; Cristo, o la Palabra aquí mencionada, es realmente Dios.

29 Hay otros lugares en las Escrituras donde tenemos un cambio repentino de persona. Por ejemplo, Salmo 2:6-7: "Aún he puesto a mi rey sobre mi santo monte de Sión. Hablaré del decreto: Jehová me dijo: Mi Hijo eres tú". Allí el primer verso representa al Padre hablando acerca del Hijo: y el segundo verso, el Hijo acerca del Padre. La razón del cambio repentino de personas en este breve pasaje es que las dos personas son un solo Dios. Puede ser que cuando nuestro texto declara que uno es imagen de Dios, la referencia sea a Cristo; y que cuando dice que uno sostiene todas las cosas por su palabra, se hace referencia al Padre, no haciéndose designación alguna porque los dos son un solo Dios sin distinción.

 30 Si esta no es una conclusión satisfactoria, podríamos considerar la expresión desde esta perspectiva: podríamos entender que el término “palabra” tiene en cierto modo el significado de un evento o acto. Por ejemplo, en el Evangelio (Lucas 2:15) leemos acerca de los pastores que dijeron: “Vayamos ahora hasta Belén, y veamos esto [palabra – evento] que ha sucedido”; veamos el evento que ha tenido lugar allí. Entonces, en esta frase que declara que Cristo sostiene todas las cosas por la palabra de su poder, podríamos entender “por el acto de su poder”. Por la operación de su poder se preservan todas las cosas; y toda existencia y poder se derivan no de las cosas mismas sino del poder activo de Dios. Además, el poder y la Palabra no deben divorciarse; son identicos. Podemos decir de una palabra eficiente que su naturaleza y sustancia son el poder operativo. Ahora bien, cada uno puede adoptar el punto de vista que le parezca más plausible.

b4.en:
Hebrews 1:4

[[This sermon is deivided into two parts, one found in verses 1-6, the other at verses 7-12]]

 Third Christmas Sermon; Hebrews 1:1-12

 CHRISTMAS MORNING SERVICE.

 THE DIVINITY OF CHRIST.

 1 This is a strong, forcible, noble epistle, preeminently and emphatically teaching the great article of faith concerning the Godhead, or the divinity of Christ. The presumption that it was not written by Paul is somewhat plausible, because the style is unusually ornamental for him. Some are of the opinion it was written by Luke; others by Apollos, whom Luke represents as “mighty in the Scriptures,” opposing the Jews. Acts 18:24 and 28 . Certain it is, no epistle enforces the Scriptures with greater power than does this. Hence it is evident the author was an eminent apostolic individual, whoever he was. Now, the object of the epistle is to establish and promote faith in the divinity of Christ, and, as already stated, scarce any portion of the Bible more strongly enforces this article of our creed. We must, therefore, confine ourselves to its words and treat it in regular order, item by item.

 2 In the first place, it was the apostle’s design to bring the Jews to the Christian faith. As we shall learn, he presses them so closely they cannot deny that Christ is true God. Now, if he is God and the Son of God, and if he himself has spoken unto us and suffered for us, justice necessarily demands our faith. We have much more reason to believe in him than had the fathers who in time past believed when God spoke simply through the prophets.

 3 Paul contrasts the ancient preachers and disciples with those of later times. The prophets and Christ are the preachers, the fathers and ourselves the disciples. The Son, the Lord himself, speaks unto us; his servants the prophets spoke unto the fathers. If the fathers believed the servants, how much more readily would they have believed the Lord himself! And if we believe not the Lord, how much more reluctant would we have been to believe the servants! Thus he makes one condition argue for the other: our unbelief contrasted with the faith of the Fathers is an awful disgrace; again, the faith of the fathers in contrast with our unbelief is deserving of very great honor. Our disgrace is yet greater when we recall the fact that God spoke to the fathers, not only once, but at different times, and not only in one way, but in different ways; and yet they always believed; while we are not induced by their example to believe, even in one instance, the message of the Lord himself. Observe, Paul proceeds with a powerful discourse in the effort to convert the Jews, yet the attempt avails nothing.

 V.1. “By divers portions (at sundry times) and in divers manners,”

 4 To me the particular and unlike meaning of these two phrases is this: “By divers portions” implies the succession of many prophets, and that all prophecies were not made through one man nor at one time; “in divers manners” signifies that through each individual prophet, to say nothing of the many, God spoke in different ways at different times. For instance, at times he expressed himself in plain, definite terms; and at other times figuratively or through visions. Ezekiel portrayed the four evangelists by the four beasts. Isaiah sometimes clearly states that Christ shall be a king; at other times he alludes to him as a rod and a branch from the stem of Jesse; again, as excellent fruit of the earth.

 5 Thus the prophets speak of Christ in “divers manners.” This latter phrase, moreover, may also be understood as implying that God spoke in various ways when he gave the people of Israel temporal aid. His leading them out of Egypt by Moses was one way of speaking, and his bringing them through the Red Sea another. In his directions to David concerning warfare and other matters he spoke in a still different way. Not one declaration, but divers declarations, were made. The objects accomplished differed. But faith was always the same — at all times and with every method.

 6 How beautifully and gently the apostle invites and persuades the Jews when he reminds them of the fathers and the prophets, and of God himself! They had unbounded confidence in the record of these as they were in time past. But now they will not believe in God. They will not take to heart the fact of his speaking to the fathers, not once only, but often; not in one way, but in different ways. Yet they know well, and must confess that such was the case. They will not believe him now when he speaks at another time and in another way — a way he never before employed nor will again. The manner of speaking they ardently desire, will never be granted. God has never yet, not even in former time, spoken in a manner designated by them. That would be but to obstruct faith and frustrate God’s design. We must leave to him the time, person and manner of speaking, and be concerned only about faith.

 7 The phrase V.2. “at the end of these days” is significant. From now to the end no other manner of preaching is to be adopted. This is the last time he purposes to speak, and the last method he will employ. He has commanded — left on record — that this Word, and only this, is to be preached until the end. Paul says ( 1 Corinthians 11:26 ): “For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink the cup, ye proclaim the Lord’s death till he come.” He also arrests their expectation when he says “in these days;” they are not to look for other days to come. The clays when he speaks for the last time and in the last manner are already at hand.

 V.2. “In his Son.”

 8 Here Paul begins to extol Christ, the last teacher, speaker and apostle: with forcible and well-grounded Scriptural evidence he shows Christ as the real Son of God and Lord over all. We must first learn to truly understand the character of Christ, that he exists in a twofold nature — divine and human. This is a point where many err. Sometimes it is to manufacture fables from his words. Men apply to the divine nature the sayings really uttered with reference to his humanity; thus are they deluded by certain passages of Scripture. It is of the utmost importance first to determine which of the statements concerning Christ pertain to his divine nature and which to his human side. This settled, all else will be easily plain.

 9 But first we must answer the inquiry liable to be made, “If the voice of God today is the last message, why is it said that Elijah and Enoch shall come, opposing Antichrist?” I answer: Concerning the advent of Elijah, I hold that he will not come in a physical manner. [As to the coming of Elijah I am suspended between heaven and earth, but I am inclined to believe it will not take place bodily. However, I will not contend hard against the other view. Each may believe or not believe it, as he likes. Editions, A, C, D, E.] I well know St. Augustine has somewhere said, “The advent of Elijah and of Antichrist is firmly fixed in the belief of all Christians.” But I also know there is no statement of Scripture to substantiate his assertion. Malachi’s prophecy concerning the coming of Elijah ( Malachi 4:5 ) the angel Gabriel makes refer to John the Baptist ( Luke 1:17 ), and Christ does the same even more explicitly where he says ( Mark 9:13 ): “But I say unto you, that Elijah is come, and they have also done unto him whatsoever they would, even as it is written of him.” Now, if John is the Elijah of the prophecy, as the Lord here says he was, the prediction of Malachi is already fulfilled. And there is nothing more prophesied concerning the coming of Elijah. The statement the Lord made just previously to the one quoted, “Elijah indeed cometh first, and restoreth all things,” may be fairly interpreted to mean that Christ, referring to the office of John, practically says: “Yes, I well know Elijah must first come and restore all things, but he has already come and accomplished it.”

 10 This view is demanded by the fact that immediately after his reference to the coming and office of Elijah, Christ speaks of his own sufferings: “It is written of the Son of man, that he must suffer many things, and be set at naught.” If this prophecy concerning Christ was to be fulfilled after the coming of Elijah, then certainly Elijah must have already come. I know of nothing more to expect concerning the coming of Elijah unless it might be that his spirit will be manifest again in the power of the Word of God, as now seems probable. For I have no longer any doubt that the Pope, with the Turks, is Antichrist, whatever you may believe.

 11 To return to Christ: We assert it is essential firmly to believe Christ true God and true man; and that the Scriptures — including Christ’s own words — sometimes have reference to the divine nature of Christ and at other times to his human nature. For instance, the declaration ( John 8:58 ), “Before Abraham was born, I am,” relates to his divinity; but the statement ( Matthew 20:23 ), “To sit on my right hand, and on my left hand, is not mine to give,” recognizes his humanity, which could not help itself even on the cross. Yet some expounders have desired here to show their great skill by abstruse interpretations made to oppose the here tics. It is his human nature that says: “The Father is greater than I.” John 14:28 . Also: “How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings.” Matthew 23:37 . Again, the passage ( Mark 13:32 ) reading, “Of that day or that hour knoweth no one, not even the angels in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father,” has reference to the man Christ.

 12 The explanation which some have made, “The Son knew not; that is, he did not choose to reveal,” is superfluous. What is the advantage of that addition? The humanity of Christ, like that of any other holy mortal man, did not, at every moment, consider and utter, did not desire and note, how some made him a man with almighty power; they improperly combine the two natures and their operation. As he did not always see, hear and feel all things, so likewise he did not at every moment contemplate in his heart every matter; he recognized things as God moved him to do, as he brought them before him. Being filled with grace and wisdom, he was able to judge and to teach as occasion demanded; the Godhead, who alone sees and knows all things, was personally present in him. Finally: All reference in the Scriptures to the humiliation and exaltation of Christ must be understood of the man; for the divine nature can neither be humiliated nor exalted.

 V.2. “Whom he appointed heir of all things.”

 13 These words refer to Christ’s human nature. We must believe in his supremacy in that respect as well as in his divinity. All creatures are subservient to the man Christ. As God, he creates all As man, he creates nothing, yet all creation is subject to him. David says ( Psalm 8:6 ), “Thou hast put all things under his feet.”

 14 Christ is our Lord and our God. As God, he creates us; as Lord, we serve him and he rules over us. The apostle refers to him in this epistle as true God, and also Lord over all. Though having two different natures, he is one person. What Christ does and suffers, essentially God does and suffers. In this case only one nature is involved.

To illustrate: I speak of a “wounded man” when but a single limb is injured. The soul is not wounded, nor is the body as a whole; only a part of the body. But I speak as! do because body and soul constitute one person. Now, as I must recognize a difference between body and soul when! speak, so must I recognize the two natures of Christ. Again: It is not a misstatement if in the night I say I have no knowledge of the sun, when at the same time! have a thorough mental knowledge of it; for I have no physical vision. Similarly, Christ knows nothing concerning the last day, and at the same time has full knowledge of it.

 V.2. “Through whom also he made the worlds.”

 15 Observe, by this same Son who in his human nature is “appointed heir of all things” — by him as God, the worlds were made. He is but one person, yet with two natures of unlike operation. There is one Christ, of two natures. The terms Paul here employs are in recognition of Christ’s highest nature.

Now, the apostle plainly speaks of the Son who is appointed heir when he says that by him the world is made. If everything is made by him, he could not himself have been created. Consequently, it is plain that he is true God. For anything not created and yet existing must be God, Again, whatsoever is made must be a creature and cannot be God; for it does not exist of itself but derives its existence from its Creator. Now, all things are made by Christ, and he is not created. Hence he must have his existence from himself; not from any creature nor any creator.

 16 Furthermore, if he is a Son he is not alone, his existence necessitates a Father. Through the Son God made the world, but God cannot himself be that Son. Consequently there must be two distinct persons, the Father and the Son, yet (because) the divine nature is only one; for there cannot be more than one God. Conclusively, then, Christ with the Father is true God. In one divine substance with him, he is Creator and Maker of the world. The only difference is, one is the Son and the other the Father. And Christ is not created by the Father, as the world was created; essentially he was begotten in eternity. Nor is he inferior to the Father. He is the same in every respect except that he is begotten of the Father, and the Father not begotten of him.

 17 If these things are beyond the grasp of our reason, reason must surrender as a captive to these and like Scripture words, and believe. Could we comprehend this mystery by human reason, there would be no faith. Clearly enough, the words, “Through whom also he made the worlds,” make mentions of two Beings. And it is not less clear that the uncreated one through whom all things were made, also must be God. Just how this can be, the Scriptures do not teach. It must be received by faith.

The Scriptures speak after this fashion: “The world is created through Christ, by the Father, in the Holy Spirit”; and though the meaning is not wholly clear, and easy of comprehension, there is good reason for the language. It is employed more by way of intimation than explanation — to imply that the Father derives not his substance from the Son, but the Son from the Father; and that the latter is the first original person in the Godhead. In the statement that the Father made the world through Christ, not Christ through the Father, the intent is to teach the Father’s title to the first person; he from whom, through Christ, all things have existence. John speaks in the same way ( John 1:3 ), “All things were made through him.” And Paul again ( Colossians 1:16 ), “All things have been created through him, and unto him;” and ( Romans 11:36 ), “For of him, and through him, and unto him, are all things.

 18 Note the aptness of the language where Christ is termed an “heir,” in reference to his humanity. For who should be more entitled to inherit the estate of God than his Son? He with the Father created it — created all creatures. But Christ is man and Son, and because of his Sonship he inherits; in both natures is he Son. But as to the origin of the apostle’s particular language, we shall learn that in the Gospel.

 V.3. “Who being the effulgence [brightness] of his glory and the very image of his substance [person].”

 19 Paul uses these figures to express with all possible clearness the fact that Christ is a person distinct from the Father, yet one, real, true God. But the German and Latin words are not just equivalent to the Greek terms employed by the apostle. The apostle speaks of Christ as the effulgence proceeding from the glory of the Father. Just as the illumination of the morning sun, the sun’s vital substance, is not a part of the effulgence, but the whole effulgence of the whole sun, proceeding from the sun and yet inherent in it. By the figure, “the effulgence of his glory,” is conveyed as in a word the birth of the Son, the unity of his nature and the Father’s, and the distinction of the persons. Christ, without limit of time, is eternally begotten of the Father, and ever proceeds, with that unweariedness represented by the sun in the morning rather than at midday or evening. But Christ is not the person of the Father, as the effulgence is not the sun. He is with and in the Father; not existing before nor after, but co-eternal with him and a part of him, as the effulgence is with and a part of the sun.

 20 The apostle terms the Father’s effulgence “Doxa,” (glory) properly implying honor or glory. Therefore the divine nature is unqualified glory and honor, having all in itself and deriving nothing from another. It has the right to boast of and glory in itself. Now, Paul says Christ is complete light, the full effulgence of God’s honor. That is, he too has in himself the unlimited Godhead and has equal right with the Father to boast and glory. The only exception is, he derives his authority from the Father and not the Father from him. He is the effulgence proceeding from the paternal honor, he is God begotten and not God begetting, yet God complete and perfect as the Father is.

 21 The Scriptures, you will observe, do not so speak of the saints, though they are also an honor to God; that is, they were created for his honor. But Paul says Christ is the brightness of the paternal honor; the words force the conclusion that the brightness constitutes the Father’s honor, else it would not be the effulgence of his honor. But what shall I say by way of explanation? These words are more easily understood by the heart than explained by tongue or pen. They are in themselves clearer than any commentary renders them, and in proportion as they are explained are they obscured. The substance of the clause is this: the whole Godhead is in Christ, and to him as to God all honor is due; yet he does not derive his Godhood from himself, but from the Father. The apostle implies two persons but one God; for the Holy Spirit is not mentioned here. When we have advanced far enough to comprehend two persons existent in one God, we will readily believe in the third person.

 22 In the other figure the apostle styles Christ an image or sign of the substance of God. Despite its clearness I still claim the privilege of speaking plainly and clearly. An image created after the likeness of a person is not an image of the substance or nature of that person. It is not a being; it is mere stone or wood. It is an image formed from stone or wood substance in the likeness of man. But if I could handle the substance of the person as the potter handles clay and make therewith an image of the individual which should also perfectly contain his substance or nature, that would, as you perceive, be an essential image, or a likeness of the human substance. But such would be a creature. An image necessarily is constructed from a different substance than the thing imaged, and differs in nature.

Here the Son is such an image of the Father substance, that the Father’s substance is the image itself. If we may so express it, the image is made from the Father’s substance. The image is not only like the Father resembling him, but fully contains his whole substance and nature; as it may be said of “the effulgence of his glory,” that the effulgence is constituted of the glory, and not only like it but embodying it perfectly, making the effulgence and the glory identical.

 23 Now notice, as I say an image of man is formed of wood or stone, so I say Christ is a divine image: as truly as the former is but a material image, so truly is the latter God. Paul calls Christ the image of the living and invisible God.

In the wooden image, this perfection is lacking. Though a wooden image, it is not an image of the wood but of an individual; it does not represent the wood, but the individual. Though the individual be faithfully reproduced in the wood, yet he himself is not wood; his substance is something different from the substance imaging him. In all cases the image differs in substance from the person imaged. It is impossible to furnish an image actually the substance of the individual. But in this verse we have an image and one imaged who are identical in substance, except that the Father is not an image. The Father is not fashioned from nor like the Son; but the Son from the Father, and is like the Father, in one simple, truly divine substance with him.

 24 Such perfection is also wanting in the sun and its effulgence. The sun has its own splendor, and the same is true of its effulgence, but the effulgence derives its splendor from the sun. But in the figure before us, effulgence is splendor; of the splendor, if we may so speak, the effulgence is constituted. The splendor is essentially and perfectly the effulgence itself, with this difference that the effulgence has not its origin in itself but in the paternal splendor.

 25 You will notice the verse is even now clearer than the explanation. “The image of his substance,” “the effulgence of his glory” — these Paul’s sayings are clear enough. The tongue should be silent here to allow the heart to reflect. The Hebrew mode of speaking is thus: “Pauperes sanctorum, i. pauperes sancti; Virtus Dei, i. virtus Deus; Sic, character substantiae, 1 character substantia, subsistens et impsemet Deus; Sic, splendor gloriae, i. splendor gloria ipsa.” Latin scholars may easily comprehend this, but for the Germans and the common people it suffices to call the likeness made from gold an image of gold. Similarly, they are to call Christ an image of God the Father because he is wholly of God in character, and there is no God beside him, though at the same time his Godhead and image have origin from the Father as the first person; but the two are one God. This is not true of creatures. The golden image represents not a golden nature, but the wholly different nature of the individual Though it is a golden image, it does not image the nature of gold. Another image is necessary to represent the nature of gold; as, for instance, a golden color, or something else not truly gold.

But in our text the image is also the substance of the imaged, and no other image is requisite than its own substance. It is faith that is called for here and not keen speculation. The words are clear enough; they are positive and forcible. He who will not in them recognize the divinity of Christ, will not recognize it in any way. Christ is not here termed a common image in the ordinary sense of the word; the word used is “Character” — an image more characteristic than a portrait or any other likeness. Again, he is called “Apaugasma” — an actual brightness resembling nothing but the glory from which it proceeds.

 V.3. “And upholding all things by the word of his power.”

 26 For a third time Christ is represented as God. First, it is stated that the worlds were made by him; second, he is called the brightness and the image of God; and here he upholds all things. If he upholds all, he is not himself upheld. He is supreme, hence he must be God. To uphold all things is to support and maintain them. Not only are all things made by him, as stated in the preceding verse, but they are perpetuated and preserved by him. As Paul says in Colossians 1:17 : “In him all things consist.” The word “upholding” is well chosen. Christ neither coerces nor restrains nor disturbs the peace; he gently sustains, permitting all creatures to enjoy his tender goodness. As it is written in the Wisdom of Solomon, Song of Solomon 8:1 : “Wisdom reacheth from one end to another mightily; and sweetly doth she order all things.”

 27 I am not fully decided as to the intent of the phrase “by the word of his power.” Were these the words of uninspired man, I would think the writer in error; for Christ is himself the Word, as the Gospel teaches, and acts in obedience to no word. Did they refer to the person of the Father, it would be perfect harmony with the Scripture teaching; for the Father made all things through his Word and upholds them in that Word. As said in Psalm 33:6 , “By the word of Jehovah were the heavens made.”

 28 I withhold my view to give place to another and better one. I merely venture the opinion that the apostle’s purpose in this manner of speaking may be to emphasize the unity of the persons in one Godhead. Since they are one God, we may understand here reference to the Father; God’s action is the action of each of the three persons. God upholds all things by his Word; Christ, or the Word here mentioned, is really God.

 29 There are other places in the Scriptures where we have a sudden change of person. For instance, Psalm 2:6-7 : “Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion. I will tell of the decree: Jehovah said unto me, Thou art my Son.” There the first verse represents the Father speaking concerning the Son: and the second verse, the Son concerning the Father. The reason for the sudden change of persons in this brief passage is, the two persons are one God. It may be that when our text declares that one is the image of God, the reference is to Christ; and that when it states one upholds all things by his word, reference is to the Father, no designation being made because the two are one God without distinction.

 30 If this is not a satisfactory conclusion, we might regard the expression in this light: we might understand the term “word” as having somewhat the significance of an event or act. For instance, in the Gospel ( Luke 2:15 ) we read of the shepherds saying: “Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing [word — event] that is come to pass” — let us see the event which has taken place there. So, in this phrase declaring Christ upholds all things by the word of his power, we might understand “by the act of his power.” By the operation of his power are all things preserved; and all existence and power are derived not from the things themselves but from the active power of God. Further, power and the Word are not to be divorced; they are identical. We may say of an efficient word that its nature and substance are the operating power. Now, each may adopt the view to him most plausible.
b4.es:
Hebreos 1:4

[[Este sermón se divide en dos partes, una que se encuentra en los versículos 1-6 y la otra en los versículos 7-12]]

 Tercer Sermón de Navidad; Hebreos 1:1-12

 SERVICIO MAÑANA DE NAVIDAD.

 LA DIVINIDAD DE CRISTO.

 1 Ésta es una epístola fuerte, contundente y noble, que enseña de manera preeminente y enfática el gran artículo de fe acerca de la Deidad o la divinidad de Cristo. La presunción de que no fue escrito por Pablo es algo plausible, porque el estilo es inusualmente ornamental para él. Algunos opinan que fue escrito por Lucas; otros, por Apolos, a quien Lucas presenta como “poderoso en las Escrituras”, oponiéndose a los judíos. Hechos 18:24 y 28. Lo cierto es que ninguna epístola refuerza las Escrituras con mayor poder que ésta. Por lo tanto, es evidente que el autor era un individuo apostólico eminente, fuera quien fuera. Ahora bien, el objetivo de la epístola es establecer y promover la fe en la divinidad de Cristo y, como ya se dijo, casi ninguna porción de la Biblia refuerza con más fuerza este artículo de nuestro credo. Por lo tanto, debemos limitarnos a sus palabras y tratarlo en orden regular, punto por punto.

 2 En primer lugar, el propósito del apóstol era llevar a los judíos a la fe cristiana. Como veremos, los presiona tan estrechamente que no pueden negar que Cristo es el Dios verdadero. Ahora bien, si él es Dios y el Hijo de Dios, y si él mismo nos habló y sufrió por nosotros, la justicia exige necesariamente nuestra fe. Tenemos muchas más razones para creer en él que los padres que en el pasado creyeron cuando Dios habló simplemente a través de los profetas.

3 Pablo contrasta a los predicadores y discípulos antiguos con los de épocas posteriores. Los profetas y Cristo somos los predicadores, los padres y nosotros los discípulos. El Hijo, el Señor mismo, nos habla; sus siervos los profetas hablaron a los padres. Si los padres creyeran a los siervos, ¡cuánto más fácilmente habrían creído al Señor mismo! Y si no creemos al Señor, ¡cuánto más reacios hubiéramos sido a creer a los siervos! Así, hace que una condición abogue por la otra: nuestra incredulidad contrastada con la fe de los Padres es una terrible desgracia; Una vez más, la fe de los padres en contraste con nuestra incredulidad merece un gran honor. Nuestra desgracia es aún mayor cuando recordamos que Dios habló a los padres, no sólo una vez, sino en diferentes momentos, y no sólo de una manera, sino de diferentes maneras; y sin embargo siempre creyeron; mientras que su ejemplo no nos induce a creer, ni siquiera en un solo caso, el mensaje del Señor mismo. Observemos que Pablo prosigue con un poderoso discurso en su esfuerzo por convertir a los judíos, pero el intento no sirve de nada.

 V.1. “En diversas porciones (en distintos momentos) y de diversas maneras”.

 4 Para mí, el significado particular y diferente de estas dos frases es el siguiente: “Por diversas porciones” implica la sucesión de muchos profetas, y que todas las profecías no fueron hechas a través de un solo hombre ni al mismo tiempo; “de diversas maneras” significa que a través de cada profeta individual, por no hablar de los muchos, Dios habló de diferentes maneras en diferentes momentos. Por ejemplo, a veces se expresaba en términos claros y definidos; y otras veces en sentido figurado o mediante visiones. Ezequiel representó a los cuatro evangelistas mediante las cuatro bestias. Isaías a veces declara claramente que Cristo será rey; en otras ocasiones alude a él como vara y pámpano del tronco de Jesé; nuevamente, como excelente fruto de la tierra.

5 Así, los profetas hablan de Cristo de “diversas maneras”. Además, esta última frase también puede entenderse en el sentido de que Dios habló de diversas maneras cuando dio ayuda temporal al pueblo de Israel. El hecho de que Moisés los sacara de Egipto era una forma de hablar, y el que los llevara a través del Mar Rojo, otra. En sus instrucciones a David sobre la guerra y otros asuntos, habló de una manera aún diferente. No se hizo una sola declaración, sino diversas declaraciones. Los objetivos logrados diferían. Pero la fe fue siempre la misma, en todo momento y con todos los métodos.

 6 ¡Con qué hermosa y gentileza el apóstol invita y persuade a los judíos cuando les recuerda a los padres y a los profetas, y a Dios mismo! Tenían una confianza ilimitada en el registro de estos tal como eran en el pasado. Pero ahora no creerán en Dios. No tomarán en serio el hecho de que él hable a los padres, no sólo una vez, sino muchas veces; no de una manera, sino de diferentes maneras. Sin embargo, lo saben bien y deben confesar que ese fue el caso. No le creerán ahora cuando hable en otro momento y de otra manera, una manera que nunca antes empleó ni volverá a utilizar. La manera de hablar que desean ardientemente nunca les será concedida. Dios nunca ha hablado todavía, ni siquiera en tiempos pasados, de la manera designada por ellos. Eso no sería más que obstruir la fe y frustrar el diseño de Dios. Debemos dejarle a él el tiempo, la persona y la manera de hablar, y preocuparnos sólo de la fe.

 7 La frase V.2. “al final de estos días” es significativo. Desde ahora hasta el fin no se adoptará ninguna otra forma de predicación. Esta es la última vez que se propone hablar y el último método que empleará. Él ha ordenado (dejado constancia) que esta Palabra, y sólo ésta, debe ser predicada hasta el fin. Pablo dice (1 Corintios 11:26): “Porque todas las veces que coméis este pan y bebéis la copa, la muerte del Señor anunciáis hasta que él venga”. También detiene sus expectativas cuando dice "en estos días"; no deben esperar otros días por venir. Las arcillas en las que habla por última vez y de la última manera ya están a la mano.

 V.2. “En su Hijo”.

8 Aquí Pablo comienza a ensalzar a Cristo, el último maestro, orador y apóstol: con evidencia bíblica contundente y bien fundamentada muestra a Cristo como el verdadero Hijo de Dios y Señor de todo. Primero debemos aprender a comprender verdaderamente el carácter de Cristo, que él existe en una doble naturaleza: divina y humana. Éste es un punto en el que muchos se equivocan. A veces se trata de fabricar fábulas a partir de sus palabras. Los hombres aplican a la naturaleza divina los dichos realmente pronunciados con referencia a su humanidad; así se sienten engañados por ciertos pasajes de las Escrituras. Es de suma importancia determinar primero cuáles de las declaraciones acerca de Cristo pertenecen a su naturaleza divina y cuáles a su lado humano. Una vez resuelto esto, todo lo demás quedará fácilmente claro.

 9 Pero primero debemos responder a la pregunta que probablemente se haga: “Si la voz de Dios hoy es el último mensaje, ¿por qué se dice que Elías y Enoc vendrán oponiéndose al Anticristo?” Respondo: Respecto al advenimiento de Elías, sostengo que no vendrá físicamente. [En cuanto a la venida de Elías, estoy suspendido entre el cielo y la tierra, pero me inclino a creer que no se realizará corporalmente. Sin embargo, no me opondré duramente al otro punto de vista. Cada uno puede creerlo o no creerlo, como quiera. Ediciones, A, C, D, E.] Sé bien que San Agustín ha dicho en alguna parte: “El advenimiento de Elías y del Anticristo está firmemente fijado en la creencia de todos los cristianos”. Pero también sé que no hay ninguna declaración de las Escrituras que fundamente su afirmación. La profecía de Malaquías acerca de la venida de Elías (Malaquías 4:5) la hace el ángel Gabriel hacer referencia a Juan el Bautista (Lucas 1:17), y Cristo hace lo mismo aún más explícitamente cuando dice (Marcos 9:13): “Pero os digo que Elías ha venido, y también han hecho con él todo lo que quisieron, como está escrito de él”. Ahora bien, si Juan es el Elías de la profecía, como aquí dice el Señor que lo fue, la predicción de Malaquías ya se ha cumplido. Y no hay nada más profetizado acerca de la venida de Elías. La declaración que el Señor hizo justo antes de la citada: “Elías a la verdad viene primero y restaurará todas las cosas”, puede interpretarse justamente en el sentido de que Cristo, refiriéndose al oficio de Juan, prácticamente dice: “Sí, bien sé que Elías debe venir primero y restaurar todas las cosas, pero ya vino y lo cumplió”.

10 Este punto de vista es exigido por el hecho de que inmediatamente después de su referencia a la venida y el oficio de Elías, Cristo habla de sus propios sufrimientos: “Del Hijo del Hombre está escrito que es necesario sufrir mucho y ser despreciado”. Si esta profecía acerca de Cristo iba a cumplirse después de la venida de Elías, entonces ciertamente Elías ya debía haber venido. No sé nada más que esperar acerca de la venida de Elías a menos que su espíritu se manifieste nuevamente en el poder de la Palabra de Dios, como ahora parece probable. Porque ya no tengo ninguna duda de que el Papa, junto con los turcos, es el Anticristo, creas lo que creas.

 11 Para volver a Cristo: Afirmamos que es imprescindible creer firmemente en Cristo, verdadero Dios y verdadero hombre; y que las Escrituras –incluidas las propias palabras de Cristo– a veces hacen referencia a la naturaleza divina de Cristo y otras veces a su naturaleza humana. Por ejemplo, la declaración (Juan 8:58), “Antes que Abraham naciera, yo soy”, se relaciona con su divinidad; pero la afirmación (Mateo 20:23): “Sentarse a mi derecha y a mi izquierda no me corresponde darlo”, reconoce su humanidad, que no pudo evitarlo ni siquiera en la cruz. Sin embargo, algunos expositores han querido mostrar aquí su gran habilidad mediante abstrusas interpretaciones hechas para oponerse a los herejes. Es su naturaleza humana la que dice: “El Padre es mayor que yo”. Juan 14:28 . También: “Cuántas veces quise juntar a tus hijos, como la gallina junta a sus polluelos debajo de las alas”. Mateo 23:37 . Nuevamente, el pasaje (Marcos 13:32) que dice: “Del día y la hora nadie sabe, ni siquiera los ángeles en el cielo, ni el Hijo, sino el Padre”, se refiere al hombre Cristo.

12 La explicación que algunos han dado: "El Hijo no sabía, es decir, no quiso revelar", es superflua. ¿Cuál es la ventaja de esa adición? La humanidad de Cristo, como la de cualquier otro hombre santo y mortal, no consideró y pronunció en todo momento, no deseó y notó cómo algunos lo hacían un hombre con poder omnipotente; combinan inadecuadamente las dos naturalezas y su funcionamiento. Así como no siempre vio, oyó y sintió todas las cosas, así tampoco en todo momento contempló en su corazón cada asunto; reconocía las cosas tal como Dios le impulsaba a hacer, tal como las presentaba ante él. Lleno de gracia y sabiduría, podía juzgar y enseñar según lo exigía la ocasión; la Divinidad, que es la única que ve y conoce todas las cosas, estaba personalmente presente en él. Finalmente: Toda referencia en las Escrituras a la humillación y exaltación de Cristo debe entenderse del hombre; porque la naturaleza divina no puede ser humillada ni exaltada.

 V.2. “A quien nombró heredero de todas las cosas”.

 13 Estas palabras se refieren a la naturaleza humana de Cristo. Debemos creer en su supremacía a ese respecto así como en su divinidad. Todas las criaturas están subordinadas al hombre Cristo. Como Dios, él crea todo. Como hombre, no crea nada, pero toda la creación está sujeta a él. David dice (Salmo 8:6): “Todo lo pusiste debajo de sus pies”.

 14 Cristo es nuestro Señor y nuestro Dios. Como Dios, él nos crea; como Señor, le servimos y él nos gobierna. El apóstol se refiere a él en esta epístola como Dios verdadero y también Señor de todo. Aunque tiene dos naturalezas diferentes, es una sola persona. Lo que Cristo hace y sufre, esencialmente Dios lo hace y sufre. En este caso sólo interviene una naturaleza.

Para ilustrar: hablo de un “hombre herido” cuando sólo un miembro está herido. El alma no está herida, ni el cuerpo en su conjunto; sólo una parte del cuerpo. ¡Pero hablo como! hacer porque cuerpo y alma constituyen una sola persona. Ahora bien, como debo reconocer una diferencia entre cuerpo y alma ¡cuándo! hablo, así debo reconocer las dos naturalezas de Cristo. Nuevamente: ¡No es un error si por la noche digo que no tengo conocimiento del sol, cuando al mismo tiempo! tener un conocimiento mental profundo de ello; porque no tengo visión física. De manera similar, Cristo no sabe nada acerca del último día y al mismo tiempo tiene pleno conocimiento de él.

 V.2. “Por quien también hizo el mundo”.

15 Observemos, por este mismo Hijo que en su naturaleza humana es “constituido heredero de todas las cosas”: por él como Dios, los mundos fueron hechos. Él es sólo una persona, pero con dos naturalezas de funcionamiento diferente. Hay un Cristo, de dos naturalezas. Los términos que Pablo emplea aquí son un reconocimiento de la naturaleza más elevada de Cristo.

Ahora bien, el apóstol habla claramente del Hijo que es nombrado heredero cuando dice que por él fue hecho el mundo. Si todo es hecho por él, él mismo no podría haber sido creado. En consecuencia, es claro que él es Dios verdadero. Porque todo lo que no ha sido creado y, sin embargo, existe debe ser Dios. Además, todo lo que se hace debe ser una criatura y no puede ser Dios; porque no existe por sí mismo sino que deriva su existencia de su Creador. Ahora bien, todas las cosas son hechas por Cristo, y él no es creado. Por tanto, debe tener su existencia por sí mismo; no de ninguna criatura ni de ningún creador.

 16 Además, si es Hijo, no está solo, su existencia necesita de un Padre. Por medio del Hijo Dios hizo el mundo, pero Dios mismo no puede ser ese Hijo. Por consiguiente, es necesario que haya dos personas distintas, el Padre y el Hijo, pero (porque) la naturaleza divina es una sola; porque no puede haber más de un Dios. Entonces, de manera concluyente, Cristo con el Padre es Dios verdadero. En una sustancia divina con él, él es Creador y Hacedor del mundo. La única diferencia es que uno es el Hijo y el otro el Padre. Y Cristo no es creado por el Padre, como fue creado el mundo; esencialmente fue engendrado en la eternidad. Tampoco es inferior al Padre. Él es el mismo en todo excepto que es engendrado del Padre, y el Padre no es engendrado por él.

 17 Si estas cosas están fuera del alcance de nuestra razón, la razón debe entregarse cautiva a ellas y a las palabras de la Escritura, y creer. Si pudiéramos comprender este misterio mediante la razón humana, no habría fe. Es bastante claro que las palabras “por medio de quien también hizo los mundos” mencionan dos Seres. Y no es menos claro que el increado por quien fueron hechas todas las cosas, también debe ser Dios. Las Escrituras no enseñan cómo puede ser esto. Debe ser recibido por fe.

Las Escrituras hablan así: “El mundo es creado por Cristo, por el Padre, en el Espíritu Santo”; y aunque el significado no es del todo claro y fácil de comprender, hay buenas razones para el lenguaje. Se emplea más a modo de insinuación que de explicación, para implicar que el Padre no deriva su sustancia del Hijo, sino el Hijo del Padre; y que este último es la primera persona original en la Deidad. En la afirmación de que el Padre hizo el mundo por medio de Cristo, no Cristo por medio del Padre, la intención es enseñar el título del Padre a la primera persona; aquel de quien, por medio de Cristo, todas las cosas tienen existencia. Juan habla de la misma manera (Juan 1:3): “Todas las cosas fueron hechas por él”. Y Pablo nuevamente (Colosenses 1:16), “Todas las cosas fueron creadas por medio de él y para él”; y (Romanos 11:36), “Porque de él, por él y para él, todas las cosas son.

 18 Nótese lo acertado del lenguaje en el que a Cristo se le llama “heredero”, en referencia a su humanidad. Porque ¿quién debería tener más derecho a heredar el patrimonio de Dios que su Hijo? Él con el Padre lo creó, creó todas las criaturas. Pero Cristo es hombre e Hijo, y por su condición de Hijo hereda; en ambas naturalezas está el Hijo. Pero en cuanto al origen del lenguaje particular del apóstol, lo aprenderemos en el Evangelio.

 V.3. “Quien siendo el resplandor [brillo] de su gloria y la imagen misma de su sustancia [persona]”.

19 Pablo usa estas figuras para expresar con toda la claridad posible el hecho de que Cristo es una persona distinta del Padre, pero un solo Dios real y verdadero. Pero las palabras alemanas y latinas no son sólo equivalentes a los términos griegos empleados por el apóstol. El apóstol habla de Cristo como el resplandor que procede de la gloria del Padre. Así como la iluminación del sol de la mañana, la sustancia vital del sol, no es parte del resplandor, sino todo el resplandor de todo el sol, que procede del sol y, sin embargo, es inherente a él. Por la figura, "el resplandor de su gloria", se transmite como en una palabra el nacimiento del Hijo, la unidad de su naturaleza y la del Padre, y la distinción de las personas. Cristo, sin límite de tiempo, es eternamente engendrado del Padre, y siempre procede, con esa incansabilidad representada por el sol por la mañana en lugar de al mediodía o al anochecer. Pero Cristo no es la persona del Padre, como el resplandor no es el sol. Él está con y en el Padre; no existiendo antes ni después, sino coeterno con él y una parte de él, como el resplandor es con y una parte del sol.

 20 El apóstol denomina la refulgencia del Padre “Doxa”, (gloria), lo que implica propiamente honor o gloria. Luego la naturaleza divina es gloria y honra absolutas, que lo tiene todo en sí misma y nada deriva de otro. Tiene derecho a jactarse y gloriarse de sí mismo. Ahora, Pablo dice que Cristo es luz completa, el pleno resplandor del honor de Dios. Es decir, él también tiene en sí mismo la Deidad ilimitada y tiene igual derecho que el Padre a jactarse y gloriarse. La única excepción es que él deriva su autoridad del Padre y no el Padre de él. Él es la refulgencia procedente del honor paterno, es Dios engendrado y no Dios engendrador, pero Dios completo y perfecto como el Padre.

21 Como observaréis, las Escrituras no hablan así de los santos, aunque también son un honor para Dios; es decir, fueron creados para su honor. Pero Pablo dice que Cristo es el resplandor del honor paterno; las palabras fuerzan la conclusión de que el brillo constituye el honor del Padre, de lo contrario no sería la refulgencia de su honor. Pero ¿qué diré a modo de explicación? Estas palabras se entienden más fácilmente con el corazón que con la lengua o la pluma. Son en sí mismos más claros de lo que los hace cualquier comentario, y en la medida en que se explican, se oscurecen. La sustancia de la cláusula es esta: toda la Deidad está en Cristo, y a él como a Dios se le debe todo honor; sin embargo, no obtiene su Divinidad de sí mismo, sino del Padre. El apóstol implica dos personas pero un Dios; porque el Espíritu Santo no se menciona aquí. Cuando hayamos avanzado lo suficiente como para comprender dos personas que existen en un Dios, fácilmente creeremos en la tercera persona.

 22 En la otra figura el apóstol define a Cristo como una imagen o signo de la sustancia de Dios. A pesar de su claridad, todavía reclamo el privilegio de hablar llana y claramente. Una imagen creada a semejanza de una persona no es una imagen de la sustancia o naturaleza de esa persona. No es un ser; es mera piedra o madera. Es una imagen formada a partir de una sustancia de piedra o madera a semejanza del hombre. Pero si pudiera manipular la sustancia de la persona como el alfarero maneja el barro y hacer con ella una imagen del individuo que también contuviera perfectamente su sustancia o naturaleza, eso sería, como veis, una imagen esencial o una semejanza de la sustancia humana. Pero así sería una criatura. Una imagen se construye necesariamente a partir de una sustancia diferente a la de la cosa representada y difiere en naturaleza.

Aquí el Hijo es tal imagen de la sustancia del Padre, que la sustancia del Padre es la imagen misma. Si podemos expresarlo así, la imagen está hecha de la sustancia del Padre. La imagen no sólo es como el Padre que se le parece, sino que contiene plenamente toda su sustancia y naturaleza; como se puede decir de “el resplandor de su gloria”, que el resplandor está constituido por la gloria, y no sólo se parece a ella, sino que la encarna perfectamente, haciendo que el resplandor y la gloria sean idénticos.

23 Ahora fíjense, así como digo que la imagen del hombre está hecha de madera o de piedra, así digo que Cristo es una imagen divina: tan verdaderamente como la primera no es más que una imagen material, así verdaderamente el segundo es Dios. Pablo llama a Cristo la imagen del Dios vivo e invisible.

En la imagen de madera falta esta perfección. Aunque es una imagen de madera, no es una imagen de la madera sino de un individuo; no representa la madera, sino el individuo. Aunque el individuo esté fielmente reproducido en la madera, él mismo no es madera; su sustancia es algo diferente de la sustancia que lo representa. En todos los casos la imagen difiere sustancialmente de la persona representada. Es imposible dar una imagen de la sustancia real del individuo. Pero en este versículo tenemos una imagen y una imagen que son idénticos en sustancia, excepto que el Padre no es una imagen. El Padre no está formado a partir del Hijo ni es semejante a él; pero el Hijo proviene del Padre, y es como el Padre, en una sustancia simple y verdaderamente divina con él.

 24 Tal perfección también falta en el sol y su resplandor. El sol tiene su propio esplendor, y lo mismo ocurre con su refulgencia, pero la refulgencia deriva su esplendor del sol. Pero en la figura que tenemos ante nosotros, la refulgencia es esplendor; del esplendor, si así podemos hablar, se constituye la refulgencia. El esplendor es esencial y perfectamente el resplandor mismo, con la diferencia de que el resplandor no tiene su origen en sí mismo sino en el esplendor paterno.

25 Notarás que el versículo es incluso ahora más claro que la explicación. “La imagen de su sustancia”, “el resplandor de su gloria”: estos dichos de Pablo son bastante claros. La lengua debe guardar silencio aquí para permitir que el corazón reflexione. El modo hebreo de hablar es así: "Pauperes sanctorum, i. pauperes sancti; Virtus Dei, i. virtus Deus; Sic, carácter substantiae, 1 carácter sustancia, subsistens et impsemet Deus; Sic, splendor gloriae, i. splendor gloria ipsa". Los estudiosos del latín pueden comprenderlo fácilmente, pero para los alemanes y la gente común es suficiente llamar imagen de oro a la imagen hecha de oro. De manera similar, deben llamar a Cristo una imagen de Dios Padre porque él es totalmente de Dios en carácter, y no hay Dios fuera de él, aunque al mismo tiempo su Divinidad e imagen tienen origen en el Padre como la primera persona; pero los dos son un solo Dios. Esto no es cierto para las criaturas. La imagen dorada no representa una naturaleza dorada, sino la naturaleza completamente diferente del individuo. Aunque es una imagen dorada, no representa la naturaleza del oro. Es necesaria otra imagen para representar la naturaleza del oro; como, por ejemplo, un color dorado o algo que no sea verdaderamente dorado.

Pero en nuestro texto la imagen es también la sustancia de lo imaginado, y no se requiere ninguna otra imagen que su propia sustancia. Lo que se necesita aquí es fe y no especulaciones entusiastas. Las palabras son bastante claras; son positivos y contundentes. El que no quiera reconocer en ellos la divinidad de Cristo, no la reconocerá de ninguna manera. Aquí no se denomina a Cristo una imagen común en el sentido ordinario de la palabra; la palabra utilizada es "Personaje", una imagen más característica que un retrato o cualquier otra semejanza. Nuevamente se le llama “Apaugasma”, un brillo real que no se parece más que a la gloria de la que procede.

 V.3. “Y sustentando todas las cosas con la palabra de su poder”.

26 Por tercera vez Cristo es representado como Dios. Primero, se afirma que los mundos fueron hechos por él; segundo, se le llama resplandor e imagen de Dios; y aquí él sostiene todas las cosas. Si lo sostiene todo, él mismo no es sostenido. Él es supremo, por lo tanto debe ser Dios. Sostener todas las cosas es apoyarlas y mantenerlas. No sólo todas las cosas son hechas por él, como se dice en el versículo anterior, sino que también son perpetuadas y preservadas por él. Como dice Pablo en Colosenses 1:17: “En él todas las cosas subsisten”. La palabra “sostener” está bien elegida. Cristo ni coacciona ni restringe ni perturba la paz; él sostiene suavemente, permitiendo que todas las criaturas disfruten de su tierna bondad. Como está escrito en La Sabiduría de Salomón, Cantares de los Cantares 8:1: “La sabiduría se extiende poderosamente de un extremo a otro, y todo lo ordena dulcemente”.

 27 No estoy completamente decidido en cuanto a la intención de la frase “por la palabra de su poder”. Si estas fueran las palabras de un hombre sin inspiración, pensaría que el escritor está equivocado; porque Cristo es él mismo la Palabra, como enseña el Evangelio, y no actúa sin obedecer ninguna palabra. Si se refirieran a la persona del Padre, estaría en perfecta armonía con la enseñanza de las Escrituras; porque el Padre hizo todas las cosas por su Palabra y las sostiene en esa Palabra. Como se dice en el Salmo 33:6: “Por la palabra de Jehová fueron hechos los cielos”.

 28 Retengo mi punto de vista para dar lugar a otro y mejor. Simplemente aventuro la opinión de que el propósito del apóstol al hablar de esta manera puede ser enfatizar la unidad de las personas en una sola Deidad. Dado que son un solo Dios, podemos entender aquí una referencia al Padre; La acción de Dios es la acción de cada una de las tres personas. Dios sostiene todas las cosas por su Palabra; Cristo, o la Palabra aquí mencionada, es realmente Dios.

29 Hay otros lugares en las Escrituras donde tenemos un cambio repentino de persona. Por ejemplo, Salmo 2:6-7: "Aún he puesto a mi rey sobre mi santo monte de Sión. Hablaré del decreto: Jehová me dijo: Mi Hijo eres tú". Allí el primer verso representa al Padre hablando acerca del Hijo: y el segundo verso, el Hijo acerca del Padre. La razón del cambio repentino de personas en este breve pasaje es que las dos personas son un solo Dios. Puede ser que cuando nuestro texto declara que uno es imagen de Dios, la referencia sea a Cristo; y que cuando dice que uno sostiene todas las cosas por su palabra, se hace referencia al Padre, no haciéndose designación alguna porque los dos son un solo Dios sin distinción.

 30 Si esta no es una conclusión satisfactoria, podríamos considerar la expresión desde esta perspectiva: podríamos entender que el término “palabra” tiene en cierto modo el significado de un evento o acto. Por ejemplo, en el Evangelio (Lucas 2:15) leemos acerca de los pastores que dijeron: “Vayamos ahora hasta Belén, y veamos esto [palabra – evento] que ha sucedido”; veamos el evento que ha tenido lugar allí. Entonces, en esta frase que declara que Cristo sostiene todas las cosas por la palabra de su poder, podríamos entender “por el acto de su poder”. Por la operación de su poder se preservan todas las cosas; y toda existencia y poder se derivan no de las cosas mismas sino del poder activo de Dios. Además, el poder y la Palabra no deben divorciarse; son identicos. Podemos decir de una palabra eficiente que su naturaleza y sustancia son el poder operativo. Ahora bien, cada uno puede adoptar el punto de vista que le parezca más plausible.

b5.en:
Hebrews 1:5

[[This sermon is deivided into two parts, one found in verses 1-6, the other at verses 7-12]]

 Third Christmas Sermon; Hebrews 1:1-12

 CHRISTMAS MORNING SERVICE.

 THE DIVINITY OF CHRIST.

 1 This is a strong, forcible, noble epistle, preeminently and emphatically teaching the great article of faith concerning the Godhead, or the divinity of Christ. The presumption that it was not written by Paul is somewhat plausible, because the style is unusually ornamental for him. Some are of the opinion it was written by Luke; others by Apollos, whom Luke represents as “mighty in the Scriptures,” opposing the Jews. Acts 18:24 and 28 . Certain it is, no epistle enforces the Scriptures with greater power than does this. Hence it is evident the author was an eminent apostolic individual, whoever he was. Now, the object of the epistle is to establish and promote faith in the divinity of Christ, and, as already stated, scarce any portion of the Bible more strongly enforces this article of our creed. We must, therefore, confine ourselves to its words and treat it in regular order, item by item.

 2 In the first place, it was the apostle’s design to bring the Jews to the Christian faith. As we shall learn, he presses them so closely they cannot deny that Christ is true God. Now, if he is God and the Son of God, and if he himself has spoken unto us and suffered for us, justice necessarily demands our faith. We have much more reason to believe in him than had the fathers who in time past believed when God spoke simply through the prophets.

 3 Paul contrasts the ancient preachers and disciples with those of later times. The prophets and Christ are the preachers, the fathers and ourselves the disciples. The Son, the Lord himself, speaks unto us; his servants the prophets spoke unto the fathers. If the fathers believed the servants, how much more readily would they have believed the Lord himself! And if we believe not the Lord, how much more reluctant would we have been to believe the servants! Thus he makes one condition argue for the other: our unbelief contrasted with the faith of the Fathers is an awful disgrace; again, the faith of the fathers in contrast with our unbelief is deserving of very great honor. Our disgrace is yet greater when we recall the fact that God spoke to the fathers, not only once, but at different times, and not only in one way, but in different ways; and yet they always believed; while we are not induced by their example to believe, even in one instance, the message of the Lord himself. Observe, Paul proceeds with a powerful discourse in the effort to convert the Jews, yet the attempt avails nothing.

 V.1. “By divers portions (at sundry times) and in divers manners,”

 4 To me the particular and unlike meaning of these two phrases is this: “By divers portions” implies the succession of many prophets, and that all prophecies were not made through one man nor at one time; “in divers manners” signifies that through each individual prophet, to say nothing of the many, God spoke in different ways at different times. For instance, at times he expressed himself in plain, definite terms; and at other times figuratively or through visions. Ezekiel portrayed the four evangelists by the four beasts. Isaiah sometimes clearly states that Christ shall be a king; at other times he alludes to him as a rod and a branch from the stem of Jesse; again, as excellent fruit of the earth.

 5 Thus the prophets speak of Christ in “divers manners.” This latter phrase, moreover, may also be understood as implying that God spoke in various ways when he gave the people of Israel temporal aid. His leading them out of Egypt by Moses was one way of speaking, and his bringing them through the Red Sea another. In his directions to David concerning warfare and other matters he spoke in a still different way. Not one declaration, but divers declarations, were made. The objects accomplished differed. But faith was always the same — at all times and with every method.

 6 How beautifully and gently the apostle invites and persuades the Jews when he reminds them of the fathers and the prophets, and of God himself! They had unbounded confidence in the record of these as they were in time past. But now they will not believe in God. They will not take to heart the fact of his speaking to the fathers, not once only, but often; not in one way, but in different ways. Yet they know well, and must confess that such was the case. They will not believe him now when he speaks at another time and in another way — a way he never before employed nor will again. The manner of speaking they ardently desire, will never be granted. God has never yet, not even in former time, spoken in a manner designated by them. That would be but to obstruct faith and frustrate God’s design. We must leave to him the time, person and manner of speaking, and be concerned only about faith.

 7 The phrase V.2. “at the end of these days” is significant. From now to the end no other manner of preaching is to be adopted. This is the last time he purposes to speak, and the last method he will employ. He has commanded — left on record — that this Word, and only this, is to be preached until the end. Paul says ( 1 Corinthians 11:26 ): “For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink the cup, ye proclaim the Lord’s death till he come.” He also arrests their expectation when he says “in these days;” they are not to look for other days to come. The clays when he speaks for the last time and in the last manner are already at hand.

 V.2. “In his Son.”

 8 Here Paul begins to extol Christ, the last teacher, speaker and apostle: with forcible and well-grounded Scriptural evidence he shows Christ as the real Son of God and Lord over all. We must first learn to truly understand the character of Christ, that he exists in a twofold nature — divine and human. This is a point where many err. Sometimes it is to manufacture fables from his words. Men apply to the divine nature the sayings really uttered with reference to his humanity; thus are they deluded by certain passages of Scripture. It is of the utmost importance first to determine which of the statements concerning Christ pertain to his divine nature and which to his human side. This settled, all else will be easily plain.

 9 But first we must answer the inquiry liable to be made, “If the voice of God today is the last message, why is it said that Elijah and Enoch shall come, opposing Antichrist?” I answer: Concerning the advent of Elijah, I hold that he will not come in a physical manner. [As to the coming of Elijah I am suspended between heaven and earth, but I am inclined to believe it will not take place bodily. However, I will not contend hard against the other view. Each may believe or not believe it, as he likes. Editions, A, C, D, E.] I well know St. Augustine has somewhere said, “The advent of Elijah and of Antichrist is firmly fixed in the belief of all Christians.” But I also know there is no statement of Scripture to substantiate his assertion. Malachi’s prophecy concerning the coming of Elijah ( Malachi 4:5 ) the angel Gabriel makes refer to John the Baptist ( Luke 1:17 ), and Christ does the same even more explicitly where he says ( Mark 9:13 ): “But I say unto you, that Elijah is come, and they have also done unto him whatsoever they would, even as it is written of him.” Now, if John is the Elijah of the prophecy, as the Lord here says he was, the prediction of Malachi is already fulfilled. And there is nothing more prophesied concerning the coming of Elijah. The statement the Lord made just previously to the one quoted, “Elijah indeed cometh first, and restoreth all things,” may be fairly interpreted to mean that Christ, referring to the office of John, practically says: “Yes, I well know Elijah must first come and restore all things, but he has already come and accomplished it.”

 10 This view is demanded by the fact that immediately after his reference to the coming and office of Elijah, Christ speaks of his own sufferings: “It is written of the Son of man, that he must suffer many things, and be set at naught.” If this prophecy concerning Christ was to be fulfilled after the coming of Elijah, then certainly Elijah must have already come. I know of nothing more to expect concerning the coming of Elijah unless it might be that his spirit will be manifest again in the power of the Word of God, as now seems probable. For I have no longer any doubt that the Pope, with the Turks, is Antichrist, whatever you may believe.

 11 To return to Christ: We assert it is essential firmly to believe Christ true God and true man; and that the Scriptures — including Christ’s own words — sometimes have reference to the divine nature of Christ and at other times to his human nature. For instance, the declaration ( John 8:58 ), “Before Abraham was born, I am,” relates to his divinity; but the statement ( Matthew 20:23 ), “To sit on my right hand, and on my left hand, is not mine to give,” recognizes his humanity, which could not help itself even on the cross. Yet some expounders have desired here to show their great skill by abstruse interpretations made to oppose the here tics. It is his human nature that says: “The Father is greater than I.” John 14:28 . Also: “How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings.” Matthew 23:37 . Again, the passage ( Mark 13:32 ) reading, “Of that day or that hour knoweth no one, not even the angels in heaven, neither the Son, but the Father,” has reference to the man Christ.

 12 The explanation which some have made, “The Son knew not; that is, he did not choose to reveal,” is superfluous. What is the advantage of that addition? The humanity of Christ, like that of any other holy mortal man, did not, at every moment, consider and utter, did not desire and note, how some made him a man with almighty power; they improperly combine the two natures and their operation. As he did not always see, hear and feel all things, so likewise he did not at every moment contemplate in his heart every matter; he recognized things as God moved him to do, as he brought them before him. Being filled with grace and wisdom, he was able to judge and to teach as occasion demanded; the Godhead, who alone sees and knows all things, was personally present in him. Finally: All reference in the Scriptures to the humiliation and exaltation of Christ must be understood of the man; for the divine nature can neither be humiliated nor exalted.

 V.2. “Whom he appointed heir of all things.”

 13 These words refer to Christ’s human nature. We must believe in his supremacy in that respect as well as in his divinity. All creatures are subservient to the man Christ. As God, he creates all As man, he creates nothing, yet all creation is subject to him. David says ( Psalm 8:6 ), “Thou hast put all things under his feet.”

 14 Christ is our Lord and our God. As God, he creates us; as Lord, we serve him and he rules over us. The apostle refers to him in this epistle as true God, and also Lord over all. Though having two different natures, he is one person. What Christ does and suffers, essentially God does and suffers. In this case only one nature is involved.

To illustrate: I speak of a “wounded man” when but a single limb is injured. The soul is not wounded, nor is the body as a whole; only a part of the body. But I speak as! do because body and soul constitute one person. Now, as I must recognize a difference between body and soul when! speak, so must I recognize the two natures of Christ. Again: It is not a misstatement if in the night I say I have no knowledge of the sun, when at the same time! have a thorough mental knowledge of it; for I have no physical vision. Similarly, Christ knows nothing concerning the last day, and at the same time has full knowledge of it.

 V.2. “Through whom also he made the worlds.”

 15 Observe, by this same Son who in his human nature is “appointed heir of all things” — by him as God, the worlds were made. He is but one person, yet with two natures of unlike operation. There is one Christ, of two natures. The terms Paul here employs are in recognition of Christ’s highest nature.

Now, the apostle plainly speaks of the Son who is appointed heir when he says that by him the world is made. If everything is made by him, he could not himself have been created. Consequently, it is plain that he is true God. For anything not created and yet existing must be God, Again, whatsoever is made must be a creature and cannot be God; for it does not exist of itself but derives its existence from its Creator. Now, all things are made by Christ, and he is not created. Hence he must have his existence from himself; not from any creature nor any creator.

 16 Furthermore, if he is a Son he is not alone, his existence necessitates a Father. Through the Son God made the world, but God cannot himself be that Son. Consequently there must be two distinct persons, the Father and the Son, yet (because) the divine nature is only one; for there cannot be more than one God. Conclusively, then, Christ with the Father is true God. In one divine substance with him, he is Creator and Maker of the world. The only difference is, one is the Son and the other the Father. And Christ is not created by the Father, as the world was created; essentially he was begotten in eternity. Nor is he inferior to the Father. He is the same in every respect except that he is begotten of the Father, and the Father not begotten of him.

 17 If these things are beyond the grasp of our reason, reason must surrender as a captive to these and like Scripture words, and believe. Could we comprehend this mystery by human reason, there would be no faith. Clearly enough, the words, “Through whom also he made the worlds,” make mentions of two Beings. And it is not less clear that the uncreated one through whom all things were made, also must be God. Just how this can be, the Scriptures do not teach. It must be received by faith.

The Scriptures speak after this fashion: “The world is created through Christ, by the Father, in the Holy Spirit”; and though the meaning is not wholly clear, and easy of comprehension, there is good reason for the language. It is employed more by way of intimation than explanation — to imply that the Father derives not his substance from the Son, but the Son from the Father; and that the latter is the first original person in the Godhead. In the statement that the Father made the world through Christ, not Christ through the Father, the intent is to teach the Father’s title to the first person; he from whom, through Christ, all things have existence. John speaks in the same way ( John 1:3 ), “All things were made through him.” And Paul again ( Colossians 1:16 ), “All things have been created through him, and unto him;” and ( Romans 11:36 ), “For of him, and through him, and unto him, are all things.

 18 Note the aptness of the language where Christ is termed an “heir,” in reference to his humanity. For who should be more entitled to inherit the estate of God than his Son? He with the Father created it — created all creatures. But Christ is man and Son, and because of his Sonship he inherits; in both natures is he Son. But as to the origin of the apostle’s particular language, we shall learn that in the Gospel.

 V.3. “Who being the effulgence [brightness] of his glory and the very image of his substance [person].”

 19 Paul uses these figures to express with all possible clearness the fact that Christ is a person distinct from the Father, yet one, real, true God. But the German and Latin words are not just equivalent to the Greek terms employed by the apostle. The apostle speaks of Christ as the effulgence proceeding from the glory of the Father. Just as the illumination of the morning sun, the sun’s vital substance, is not a part of the effulgence, but the whole effulgence of the whole sun, proceeding from the sun and yet inherent in it. By the figure, “the effulgence of his glory,” is conveyed as in a word the birth of the Son, the unity of his nature and the Father’s, and the distinction of the persons. Christ, without limit of time, is eternally begotten of the Father, and ever proceeds, with that unweariedness represented by the sun in the morning rather than at midday or evening. But Christ is not the person of the Father, as the effulgence is not the sun. He is with and in the Father; not existing before nor after, but co-eternal with him and a part of him, as the effulgence is with and a part of the sun.

 20 The apostle terms the Father’s effulgence “Doxa,” (glory) properly implying honor or glory. Therefore the divine nature is unqualified glory and honor, having all in itself and deriving nothing from another. It has the right to boast of and glory in itself. Now, Paul says Christ is complete light, the full effulgence of God’s honor. That is, he too has in himself the unlimited Godhead and has equal right with the Father to boast and glory. The only exception is, he derives his authority from the Father and not the Father from him. He is the effulgence proceeding from the paternal honor, he is God begotten and not God begetting, yet God complete and perfect as the Father is.

 21 The Scriptures, you will observe, do not so speak of the saints, though they are also an honor to God; that is, they were created for his honor. But Paul says Christ is the brightness of the paternal honor; the words force the conclusion that the brightness constitutes the Father’s honor, else it would not be the effulgence of his honor. But what shall I say by way of explanation? These words are more easily understood by the heart than explained by tongue or pen. They are in themselves clearer than any commentary renders them, and in proportion as they are explained are they obscured. The substance of the clause is this: the whole Godhead is in Christ, and to him as to God all honor is due; yet he does not derive his Godhood from himself, but from the Father. The apostle implies two persons but one God; for the Holy Spirit is not mentioned here. When we have advanced far enough to comprehend two persons existent in one God, we will readily believe in the third person.

 22 In the other figure the apostle styles Christ an image or sign of the substance of God. Despite its clearness I still claim the privilege of speaking plainly and clearly. An image created after the likeness of a person is not an image of the substance or nature of that person. It is not a being; it is mere stone or wood. It is an image formed from stone or wood substance in the likeness of man. But if I could handle the substance of the person as the potter handles clay and make therewith an image of the individual which should also perfectly contain his substance or nature, that would, as you perceive, be an essential image, or a likeness of the human substance. But such would be a creature. An image necessarily is constructed from a different substance than the thing imaged, and differs in nature.

Here the Son is such an image of the Father substance, that the Father’s substance is the image itself. If we may so express it, the image is made from the Father’s substance. The image is not only like the Father resembling him, but fully contains his whole substance and nature; as it may be said of “the effulgence of his glory,” that the effulgence is constituted of the glory, and not only like it but embodying it perfectly, making the effulgence and the glory identical.

 23 Now notice, as I say an image of man is formed of wood or stone, so I say Christ is a divine image: as truly as the former is but a material image, so truly is the latter God. Paul calls Christ the image of the living and invisible God.

In the wooden image, this perfection is lacking. Though a wooden image, it is not an image of the wood but of an individual; it does not represent the wood, but the individual. Though the individual be faithfully reproduced in the wood, yet he himself is not wood; his substance is something different from the substance imaging him. In all cases the image differs in substance from the person imaged. It is impossible to furnish an image actually the substance of the individual. But in this verse we have an image and one imaged who are identical in substance, except that the Father is not an image. The Father is not fashioned from nor like the Son; but the Son from the Father, and is like the Father, in one simple, truly divine substance with him.

 24 Such perfection is also wanting in the sun and its effulgence. The sun has its own splendor, and the same is true of its effulgence, but the effulgence derives its splendor from the sun. But in the figure before us, effulgence is splendor; of the splendor, if we may so speak, the effulgence is constituted. The splendor is essentially and perfectly the effulgence itself, with this difference that the effulgence has not its origin in itself but in the paternal splendor.

 25 You will notice the verse is even now clearer than the explanation. “The image of his substance,” “the effulgence of his glory” — these Paul’s sayings are clear enough. The tongue should be silent here to allow the heart to reflect. The Hebrew mode of speaking is thus: “Pauperes sanctorum, i. pauperes sancti; Virtus Dei, i. virtus Deus; Sic, character substantiae, 1 character substantia, subsistens et impsemet Deus; Sic, splendor gloriae, i. splendor gloria ipsa.” Latin scholars may easily comprehend this, but for the Germans and the common people it suffices to call the likeness made from gold an image of gold. Similarly, they are to call Christ an image of God the Father because he is wholly of God in character, and there is no God beside him, though at the same time his Godhead and image have origin from the Father as the first person; but the two are one God. This is not true of creatures. The golden image represents not a golden nature, but the wholly different nature of the individual Though it is a golden image, it does not image the nature of gold. Another image is necessary to represent the nature of gold; as, for instance, a golden color, or something else not truly gold.

But in our text the image is also the substance of the imaged, and no other image is requisite than its own substance. It is faith that is called for here and not keen speculation. The words are clear enough; they are positive and forcible. He who will not in them recognize the divinity of Christ, will not recognize it in any way. Christ is not here termed a common image in the ordinary sense of the word; the word used is “Character” — an image more characteristic than a portrait or any other likeness. Again, he is called “Apaugasma” — an actual brightness resembling nothing but the glory from which it proceeds.

 V.3. “And upholding all things by the word of his power.”

 26 For a third time Christ is represented as God. First, it is stated that the worlds were made by him; second, he is called the brightness and the image of God; and here he upholds all things. If he upholds all, he is not himself upheld. He is supreme, hence he must be God. To uphold all things is to support and maintain them. Not only are all things made by him, as stated in the preceding verse, but they are perpetuated and preserved by him. As Paul says in Colossians 1:17 : “In him all things consist.” The word “upholding” is well chosen. Christ neither coerces nor restrains nor disturbs the peace; he gently sustains, permitting all creatures to enjoy his tender goodness. As it is written in the Wisdom of Solomon, Song of Solomon 8:1 : “Wisdom reacheth from one end to another mightily; and sweetly doth she order all things.”

 27 I am not fully decided as to the intent of the phrase “by the word of his power.” Were these the words of uninspired man, I would think the writer in error; for Christ is himself the Word, as the Gospel teaches, and acts in obedience to no word.
